exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Sphere Using Spherical Coordinates

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: \sqrt2 \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \sqrt2\cos\phi \big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)$ above parametrizes the sphere defined in Cartesian coordinates as $x^2+y^2+z^2=2.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
The given equation generates a sphere of radius $\sqrt2$ centered at the origin. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation $\rho =\sqrt2.$

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found using the following formulas: \[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \rho \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho \cos\phi \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \sqrt2\cdot \cos\theta\sin\phi, \:\sqrt2\cdot\sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \sqrt2\cdot\cos\phi \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle {\color{blue}\sqrt2 \cos\theta\sin\phi}, \: { \sqrt2 \sin\theta\sin\phi}, \: \sqrt2 \cos\phi \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in [-\pi,\pi].$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} \sqrt2\cos\theta\sin\phi}.$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)$ above parametrizes the sphere defined in Cartesian coordinates as $x^2+y^2+z^2=5.$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of an Ellipsoid Using Spherical Coordinates

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle 5\cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \text{_____} , \: 7\cos\phi\big\rangle \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)$ above parametrizes the ellipsoid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}+\dfrac{z^2}{49}=1.$ What is the second component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following substitution:

\[ x = 5X, \qquad y =4 Y, \qquad z = 7Z \]

Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our ellipsoid, we get

\[ X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1, \]

which is the equation of a sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin in $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation $\rho =1.$

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas: \[ X = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Z = \rho\cos\phi. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 5X,4Y, 7Z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 5\rho \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: 4\rho \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: 7\rho \cos\phi \right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 5\cdot 1\cdot \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: 4\cdot 1\cdot \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: 7\cdot 1\cdot \cos\phi \right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 5\cos\theta\sin\phi, \:{\color{blue}4\sin\theta\sin\phi}, \: 7\cos\phi \right\rangle \end{align*}

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in [-\pi,\pi].$

Therefore, the second component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}4\sin\theta\sin\phi}.$

question.explanation:
First, we make the following substitution:

\[ x = 4X, \qquad y = Y, \qquad z = 3Z \]

Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our ellipsoid, we get

\[ X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1, \]

which is the equation of a sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin in $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation $\rho =1.$

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas: \[ X = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad Z = \rho\cos\phi. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 4X,Y, 3Z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 4\rho \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: 3\rho \cos\phi \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 4\cdot 1\cdot \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: 1\cdot \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: 3\cdot 1 \cdot \cos\phi \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 4\cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: {\color{blue}3\cos\phi} \big\rangle \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Cone Using Cylindrical Coordinates

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: r\sin\theta, \: r \big\rangle, \qquad r \geq 0 \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(r,\theta)$ above parametrizes the half-cone defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z^2=x^2+y^2$ for $z\geq 0.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
In cylindrical polar coordinates, the given half-cone has the equation

\[ z = r. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its $(x,y,z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas:

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle r\cos\theta, \: r\sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle {\color{blue} r\cos\theta}, \: r\sin\theta, \: r \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $r \in [0,\infty)$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} r\cos\theta}.$

example.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Cone Using Cylindrical Coordinates

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) = \big\langle \: 5r\cos\theta,r, \: \text{_____}\big\rangle, \qquad r \geq 0 \]

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(r,\theta)$ above parametrizes the half-cone defined in Cartesian coordinates as $y^2=\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{z^2}{9}.$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{f}?$
question.explanation:
First, substituting

\[ x = 5X, \qquad y = Z, \qquad z = 3Y \]

into our equation, we get the cone whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis:

\[ Z^2=X^2+Y^2 \]

In cylindrical polar coordinates, this cone has the equation

\[ Z = r. \]

If $(r, \theta, Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(X,Y,Z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = Z. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) &= \langle x,y,z \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 5X,\: Z,\:3Y \rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 5\cdot r\cos\theta, \: r, 3\cdot r\sin\theta \big\rangle \\[3pt] &= \big\langle 5 r\cos\theta, \: r, \: {\color{blue}3r\sin\theta} \big\rangle \end{align*}

where $r \in [0,\infty)$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi).$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} 3r\sin\theta}.$

question.explanation:

\[ x = 4 X, \qquad y = 4 Y, \qquad z = Z \]

If $(r, \theta, Z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point, then its $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas:

\[ X = r\cos\theta, \qquad Y = r\sin\theta, \qquad Z = Z. \]

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) &= \left\langle x,y,z\right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 4X,\:4Y\!, \:Z \right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 4r\cos\theta, \: 4r\sin\theta, \: Z \right\rangle \\[3pt] &=\left\langle {\color{blue} 4r\cos\theta}, \: 4r\sin\theta, \: r \right\rangle \end{align*}

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue} 4r\cos\theta}.$
